title: Domain Expansion: A Latent Space Construction Framework for Multi-Task Learning
claim: Standard joint training forces objectives to share a small overlapping region; assigning each objective its own orthogonal axis removes interference.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, dashed divider, overlapping ellipses versus 3-D orthogonal axes
description: Two panels split by a vertical dashed line. Panel (a), titled 'Latent representation collapse', shows three large overlapping ellipses: red for Concept 1, blue for Concept 2 and green for Concept 3. Their small common intersection is shaded purple. A black arrow points to it with the italic label 'Limited representations satisfy all concepts'. Panel (b), titled 'Ours (Domain Expansion)', shows a 3-D coordinate frame. Red, blue and green axes for Concepts 1, 2 and 3 are mutually orthogonal, set against a large purple gradient cube or plane. Yellow dots sit in the space with dashed projection lines onto the axes. The italic label reads 'All representations satisfy all concepts'. Color coding stays consistent across panels, and the eye goes first to the purple regions.
caption: (a) Latent representation collapse. In standard multi-task learning, competing objectives lead to latent representation collapse, where the solution spaces for different concepts (colored ellipses) overlap in only a small, compromised region. (b) Domain Expansion. In contrast, our method assigns each concept to an orthogonal basis vector in the latent space, preventing interference and creating a structured, interpretable representation where features for each concept are clearly separated.
abstract: Training a single network with multiple objectives often leads to conflicting gradients that degrade shared representations, forcing them into a compromised state that is suboptimal for any single task--a problem we term latent representation collapse. We introduce Domain Expansion, a framework that prevents these conflicts by restructuring the latent space itself. Our framework uses a novel orthogonal pooling mechanism to construct a latent space where each objective is assigned to a mutually orthogonal subspace. We validate our approach across diverse benchmarks--including ShapeNet, MPIIGaze, and Rotated MNIST--on challenging multi-objective problems combining classification with pose and gaze estimation. Our experiments demonstrate that this structure not only prevents collapse but also yields an explicit, interpretable, and compositional latent space where concepts can be directly manipulated.
